walkthroughs.h2: March on Washington and Kennedy assassination
walkthroughs.body_html: The March on Washington on 28 August 1963 united labour and civil rights groups behind A. Philip Randolph and Bayard Rustin. King's 'I Have a Dream' speech became iconic. Kennedy's assassination on 22 November 1963 brought Lyndon Johnson, who used his Senate skills to break the Senate filibuster after 60 days, securing the Civil Rights Act of 2 July 1964.

walkthroughs.h2: Selma and the Voting Rights Act
walkthroughs.body_html: SNCC and SCLC focused on Selma, Alabama, where only 1 per cent of Black adults were registered. The first march on 7 March 1965 was attacked at the Edmund Pettus Bridge ('Bloody Sunday'). Johnson addressed Congress on 15 March, declaring 'we shall overcome'. The Voting Rights Act passed and was signed on 6 August 1965; Mississippi registration rose from 6 to 60 per cent by 1968.

Traditional accounts focus on 1954-65. Jacquelyn Dowd Hall's influential 2005 article argued for a 'long civil rights movement' linking 1930s labour activism, 1960s peak and post-1965 continuations including Black Power, women's movements and Black Lives Matter (founded 2013). The 1965 Watts riot, MLK's 1968 assassination and persistent inequality complicate triumphalist narratives.

mcqs.q: How was the US civil rights movement achieved?
options: Lincoln ended segregation by signing the 14th Amendment.
Through decades of mass organising — NAACP legal work, grassroots campaigns, sit-ins, freedom rides — alongside leaders like King and Malcolm X.
Malcolm X and MLK were close allies who jointly led the March on Washington.
Martin Luther King's 'I Have a Dream' speech ended segregation.

mcqs.q: How did Malcolm X's approach differ from MLK's?
options: Malcolm X advocated violent terrorism against white Americans.
Lincoln ended segregation by signing the 14th Amendment.
MLK preached nonviolent integration; Malcolm X (until 1964) advocated black self-defence, separatism, and rejected integration as a goal — though both shifted positions over time.
Malcolm X and MLK were close allies who jointly led the March on Washington.

mcqs.q: What did Brown v Board of Education decide in 1954?
options: Lincoln ended segregation by signing the 14th Amendment.
The Supreme Court ruled that 'separate but equal' schools were inherently unequal, overturning Plessy v Ferguson and beginning legal dismantling of school segregation.
Brown v Board ended slavery in the southern states.
Brown v Board of Education immediately desegregated all schools in America.
